lead: Add up many independent random variables that all follow the same distribution, then standardize the sum. The result is approximately standard normal, whatever the original distribution looked like. That is the central limit theorem, and it is the reason the normal curve turns up where nothing was normal. It turns a sum of a hundred or a million pieces into one table lookup. Engineers use it for tolerance stack-ups, auditors for error in a ledger, pollsters for the error bar on a survey, and banks for the spread of daily UPI settlement totals.
prereq: You need: the normal curve and its table of Φ, plus the binomial distribution, from Unit 3; and 4.5, which says the sample mean closes on μ, while this chapter says how the leftover gap is spread.

sections.h3: The theorem: standardizing a sum fixes its shape

blocks.text: Take n independent random variables X₁, X₂, …, X_n with the same distribution, the same mean μ, and the same finite variance σ². Put S_n = X₁ + X₂ + … + X_n. As n grows, the distribution of the standardized sum takes one fixed shape, the standard normal, whatever the parent distribution was — uniform, exponential, binomial, anything with a finite variance.

S_n itself does not settle down: its mean nμ and its variance nσ² both grow with n. Variances of independent variables add, so Var(S_n) = nσ² and the standard deviation of S_n is σ√n. Subtract the mean and divide by that standard deviation to reach a fixed scale.

blocks.where: S_n is the sum X₁ + … + X_n; μ and σ² are the mean and variance of one term, with 0 < σ² < ∞; n is the number of terms; Z_n is the standardized sum; → means the distribution of Z_n tends to the standard normal as n → ∞.

blocks.text: To use it, convert the limits on S_n into standard units and read the table of Φ.

blocks.where: a is a limit in the units of S_n; nμ is the mean of S_n; σ√n is its standard deviation; Φ is the standard normal CDF from Unit 3, the area to the left of a z-value.

blocks.text: The sample mean is the same theorem in another dress. Since X̄_n = S_n/n, dividing top and bottom of Z_n by n moves the √n down beside σ.

blocks.where: X̄_n is the sample mean; σ/√n is the standard error of the mean, the typical size of the gap between X̄_n and μ. 4.5 says the gap closes; this formula says how the remaining gap is spread.

sections.h3: Working the numbers, and the ±0.5 correction

items: Find μ and σ for one term; compute nμ and σ√n and keep them exact.
Write the question as an interval for S_n, such as P(40 ≤ S_n ≤ 60).
If S_n counts whole items, widen each limit by 0.5: 39.5 and 60.5.
Standardize each limit with z = (limit − nμ)/(σ√n).
Read Φ at each z and subtract; symmetrical limits give 2Φ(z) − 1.

blocks.text: The normal curve is continuous and puts zero probability on any single point. A count sits on the integers. The event 40 ≤ X ≤ 60 covers the whole-number blocks 40, 41, …, 60, and the strip from 39.5 to 60.5 covers exactly those blocks and nothing else. Drop the ±0.5 and the strip is half a unit too short at each end. In the middle that costs very little; in the tail it is serious, because P(X ≤ 40) needs the whole block up to 40.5, while the normal gives area only up to 40.

sections.h3: The binomial as a special case, and how big n must be

blocks.text: The binomial is a sum of n independent Bernoulli trials: each trial is 1 with probability p and 0 with probability 1 − p, so μ = p and σ² = p(1 − p). The theorem then becomes the normal approximation to the binomial.

blocks.where: X ~ Binomial(n, p); k is an integer count of successes; k + 0.5 is the continuity correction; np is the mean of X; np(1−p) is its variance.

blocks.text: How large must n be? The usual rule of thumb is n ≥ 30. The real test is the shape of the parent, and skew is what decides. A symmetric parent needs only a handful of terms: the binomial with p = 0.5 at n = 10 already sits almost on the normal curve in the figure. A skewed parent needs far more. For the binomial the working test is np ≥ 5 and n(1−p) ≥ 5, which keeps the mean about two standard deviations from both ends; with p = 0.05 that needs n around 100. When the parent is already normal, every n is exact, not approximate.

figure.caption: The standard normal curve with the standardized binomial probabilities for n = 10 and p = 0.5. Ten dots already sit on the smooth curve; a skewed parent would need many more terms.

spec.aria: The standard normal curve with the standardized binomial probabilities for ten trials sitting almost on top of it.

examples.question: A fair coin is tossed n = 100 times and X is the number of heads. Use the central limit theorem to estimate P(40 ≤ X ≤ 60), first with the continuity correction and then without it.
steps: One toss: μ = p = 0.5 and σ² = p(1 − p) = 0.25, so σ = 0.5. X = S_100 ~ Binomial(100, 0.5).
Mean of X: nμ = 100 × 0.5 = 50 heads. Standard deviation of X: σ√n = 0.5 × √100 = 0.5 × 10 = 5 heads.
Continuity correction: heads are counted in whole numbers, so 40 ≤ X ≤ 60 becomes 39.5 ≤ X ≤ 60.5.
P ≈ Φ(2.1) − Φ(−2.1) = 2Φ(2.1) − 1 = 2(0.9821) − 1 = 0.9642; the exact normal area is 0.9643, so the table's rounding costs 0.0001.
Without the correction the limits are 40 and 60, giving z = ±2.0 and P ≈ 2(0.9772) − 1 = 0.9544 (exact 0.9545).
examples.answer: P(40 ≤ X ≤ 60) ≈ 0.9643 with the continuity correction and ≈ 0.9545 without it; the corrected value is the better estimate.
examples.check:
import math
def phi(z):
    return 0.5 * (1 + math.erf(z / math.sqrt(2)))
n, p = 100, 0.5
mu = n * p
sigma = math.sqrt(n * p * (1 - p))
z = (60.5 - mu) / sigma
print(round(z, 4))
print(round(2 * phi(z) - 1, 4))
z2 = (60 - mu) / sigma
print(round(2 * phi(z2) - 1, 4))

traps: Dividing by σ instead of σ√n. With n = 100 the z-values come out 10 times too big and the answer sounds absurdly confident.
Forgetting the ±0.5 correction when S_n counts whole items. The error is small near the mean and large in the tail.
Applying the theorem when the variance is not finite, or when the variables are dependent. A sum of standard Cauchy variables is still Cauchy at every n.
Reading 'the sum is approximately normal' as 'each X_i is normal'. The individual terms keep the parent's shape; only the standardized sum is normal.

quiz.q: State the central limit theorem for independent and identically distributed random variables.
quiz.a: Let X₁, …, X_n be iid with mean μ and finite variance σ² > 0, and S_n = X₁ + … + X_n. Then (S_n − nμ)/(σ√n) → N(0,1) in distribution as n → ∞, so P(S_n ≤ a) ≈ Φ((a − nμ)/(σ√n)).

quiz.q: Why divide the deviation S_n − nμ by σ√n rather than by σ?
quiz.a: Because Var(S_n) = nσ², so the standard deviation of S_n is σ√n, not σ. Dividing by σ√n makes the variance of Z_n equal to 1 for every n, which is the only fixed scale; dividing by σ would leave variance n and no limit.

quiz.q: Why is a ±0.5 correction needed before using the normal curve on a binomial count?
quiz.a: The count runs on the integers and the normal curve is continuous. P(X ≤ 40) must cover the block up to 40.5, so the normal limit is 40.5. Without the correction half of each end block is lost — small near the mean, large in the tail.

quiz.q: A fair die is rolled 100 times and X is the total of the faces. Estimate P(X ≤ 360) by the central limit theorem.
A coin is tossed n times and X̄ is the proportion of heads. How large must n be so that P(|X̄ − 0.5| ≤ 0.01) ≥ 0.95?
quiz.a: For one toss σ = 0.5, so the standard error is σ/√n = 0.5/√n. The 95% condition needs 1.96 × 0.5/√n ≤ 0.01, giving √n ≥ 98 and n ≥ 9604 tosses.

quiz.q: Which parent needs the largest n before its sum looks normal: uniform(0,1), exponential(1), or Bernoulli(0.05)? Justify.
quiz.a: Bernoulli(0.05). It is the most skewed: with p far from 0.5 the sum stays piled at small values for a long time. The working test np ≥ 5 needs n around 100. Uniform is symmetric and converges fastest; exponential(1) is skewed but less extreme than Bernoulli(0.05).

quiz.q: A student applies the theorem to the average of 500 independent standard Cauchy variables. What is wrong?
quiz.a: The standard Cauchy distribution has no mean and no variance, so neither nμ nor σ√n exists. The average of Cauchy variables is again Cauchy at every n — it never concentrates and never becomes normal. The theorem requires a finite σ², and that must be checked before standardizing.

beyond: Not for the exam. The error in the normal approximation shrinks like 1/√n; the Berry–Esseen bound makes this precise using the third absolute moment, and Edgeworth expansions push the error down another order. When the parent is unknown, modern practice replaces the table with the bootstrap. In engineering the same arithmetic sizes tolerance stack-ups and six-sigma limits; in software, A/B tests use the sample-mean form for lift and confidence intervals. The vector version of the theorem is in 4.7. Search 'Berry–Esseen theorem', 'Edgeworth expansion' or 'bootstrap confidence interval' to go further.
